messages.subject: N-mix survey level area offset
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have been wracking my brain to find a way to deal with variable sampling area per survey visit to a site in an N-mixture framework for birds. For instance, when I surveyed site 1 I surveyed 2 ha during visit 1, 2.1 ha during visit 2, and 1.8 ha during visit 3. The length of the site surveyed was the same, by the width varied due to tidal conditions. This seems like a good reason to use an offset in the abundance part of the N-mixture model, but how?

Below is the typical abundance part of a jags model, where you provide an offset (area surveyed) per site, though this assumes the area survey per site stays the same across visits.
# Abundance portion of model
# Likelihood
for(i in 1:n.sites) {
N[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
log(lambda[i]) <-  alpha0 + log(offset[i])
}

Is it possible to incorporate an offset (offset[i,k]) on lambda where k is the site visit?

If a visit level offset isn't possible then perhaps it doesn't make sense to use an N-mixture model when the area surveyed at each site varies between visits because if birds are stationary you would expect to count less birds when surveying less area.

 Any suggestions for analyzing repeat count data without an offset are also welcome.

Thanks in advance for any thoughts,

Jerry

messages.subject: Re: N-mix survey level area offset
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jerry,

you can include a survey-specific offset like this:

for(i in 1:n.sites) {
  for(k in 1:n.rep){
    #abundance model
    N[i,k] ~ dpois(lambda[i,k])
    log(lambda[i,k]) <-  alpha0 + log(offset[i,k])

    #detection model
    y[i,k] ~ dbin(p[i,k],N[i,k])
    logit(p[i,k]) <- alpha1
  }
}

exp(alpha0) is then the predicted abundance per unit effort (i.e. abundance/ha). You just have to think carefully about assumptions. The assumption here is that there is a constant density, thus abundance is directly proportional to area. If you are counting shore animals (you mentioned tide) they might just concentrate more during high tide but abundance stays the same (in that case you don't need an offset).

Best,

Mathias

messages.subject: RE: N-mix survey level area offset
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jerry,

intuitively, off the top of my head, I feel that a model, where N is NOT constant across occasions should be estimable, since you assume that you know exactly the manner in which the population is not closed: it is described by that offset. In that respect, there is also a section in the R&D bible which may be relevant (4.6.)

Only thing I wonder right now is whether you can really assume that density remains constant when the tidal area changes ? This is what you assume when specifying an offset. But would the birds not be expected to crowd more densely if there is less area ? In that case perhaps an analysis without offset might be more appropriate ?

Best regards  ---  Marc

messages.subject: RE: Doubts about parboot function
messages.body_plain:
Dear Isabella,

I think that if you adhere to the traditional significance testing philosophy leading to a black-and-white conclusion about the fit of a model, then anything smaller than 0.05 would indicate an ill-fitting model. However, one ought to be just as wary about too good a fit as about a too badly fitting model. Hence, too large values are also suspect. Thus, anything outside of an interval 0.05 - 0.95 (or perhaps outside of 0.025 - 0.975 ?) would indicate an ill-fitting model.

Best regards  --- Marc

Hi Marc and Jerry,

Jerry send some simple simulation code and it looks like the model I sent is not estimable without additional information that helps estimate detection probability (double observer, distance). My intuition was the same as Marc's, it should work if density is assumed constant, but apparently it does not, or at least not in that form. The situation is easier if survey effort varies across sites but is constant across surveys within sites which is described in the HM book 6.9 for constant areas but varying transect length or can be modeled with a simple offset if survey area differs. I will keep looking into this a bit more since I have a similar dataset where survey effort varies across survey occasions (I did not collect the data).

Best,

Mathias

This only happens with RStudio current versions on Mac OS. They are aware of it and are working on it for a future RStudio release but it’s been months without a solution on their end so I wouldn’t wait for that. If you do the final MCMC run in R and not RStudio it will work in parallel. There is a workaround to get the parallel processors working in RStudio that I don’t think has any noticeable slowdown of performance. You can add this to your code or even to your .rprofile
parallel:::setDefaultClusterOptions(setup_strategy = "sequential")
This might break code on a non-Mac OS if you’re a sharing it so the .Rprofile is probably a better place for it as a temporary solution.

iirc the code just sets up the socketclusters one at a time but then runs the code in parallel. I could be wrong and don’t have a Mac to try on currently. Best to give it a try on a short test run of just a few iterations per chain.

Hope that helps,
Daniel Hocking

Hi all,

Thanks for your quick responses. Denis, I think you may be right that it has to do with initial values, but I'm really struggling to troubleshoot it. Perhaps you can see what's happening in the code?

André, no NAs in the covariates, and I'm actually still having these issues when I've imputed the NAs in my response. Thus, I'm having these inconsistent parent node issues without a single NA anywhere in the data.

So, I'm trying to run a multi-season multinomial mixture model. Small mammals were trapped at 6 sites, for 4 consecutive nights, for 17 consecutive years. Every trapped mammal had its fur clipped to allow identification of recaps. I have my data organised in a c(6,4,17) array, where each value is the number of new animals caught. Thus, the data is a removal sampling type design which I've tried to analyse with the conditional multinomial model from section 7.6 in Kéry & Schaub (2015) AHM Vol. 1, extended to multiple years.

## Model 1: Conditional multinomial

str(bdata<-list(y=y[,,-14],ncap=ncap[,-14],site=nrow(y),survey=ncol(y),year=dim(y[,,-14])[3],rain=rain6[-14],rainp=rainp[-14],fire=fire[,-14])) # 14th year is removed because there's no data

# Model

cat(file="Nmulti_conditional_fuscipes.txt"," # Model for Rattus fuscipes only
    model{

    ## Priors

    # Abundance model

    alpha0 ~ dnorm(0,0.001) # Abundance intercept
    r ~ dunif(-1,1) # Annual population growth rate
    alpha1 ~ dunif(-5,5) # Effect of rainfall in past 6 mo
    alpha2 ~ dunif(-5,5) # Effect of fire history, which varies per year and site

    # Random site effect

    for(i in 1:site){
      eps[i] ~ dnorm(0,tau.l) # Random site effect on abundance
    }
    tau.l <- pow(sigma.l,-2)
    sigma.l ~ dunif(0,5)

    # Detection model

    beta0 <- logit(p0) # Convert intercept to logit scale to assign uniform prior below
    p0 ~ dunif(0,1)
    beta1 ~ dunif(-5,5) # Effect of rainfall in week before survey on capture probability

    ## Conditional multinomial cell probabilities

    for(k in 1:year){
      for(i in 1:site){
        pi[i,1,k] <- p[i,k]
        pi[i,2,k] <- p[i,k] * pow((1-p[i,k]),1)

messages.body_plain:
John, it looks like you have a typo (JAGS is case-sensitive). The pertinent parts of the error message are:

“Unknown variable nInd” – meaning nInd is used in the model statement but not provided in the data; and

“Unused variable "nind" in data” – meaning nind is supplied in the data but not used in the model statement.

If nInd and nind are referring to the same thing, changing nInd in the model statement to nind (all lower-case) should fix it.

You might want to check your use of "f" and "n.occasions" as well, as apparently those are also supplied as data but not used in the model statement (won't cause a fatal error, only a warning, but might indicate that you haven't done what you intended to do with the model).

Cheers,

Emily

Dear Thais,

looks to me like there is a missing value in Area at position (1,1) (and perhaps elsewhere, too). JAGS doesn't want missing values in a covariate. If there is a missing value in the response N at every position where there is also a missing value in Area, then I would simply replace the missing values in Area with an arbitrary number. This will not affect the likelihood, but satisfy JAGS.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject_clean: Is it possible to obtain abundance/occupancy estimates from an iterative mark resight survey
messages.body_plain:
Hello HMEcology group,

I would appreciate your feedback on the types (if any) of modeling frameworks I could use to estimate occupancy/abundance for data obtained from a mark-resight survey where the main purpose was to estimate apparent survival, but since this method yields count data when the observer is looking for the color-banded birds, I wanted to see if I can use it for that purpose too.

Attached the data structure diagram if you prefer a visual aid, here the summary:
- Sites = 8 a collection of sites selected to attempt catching-colorbanding-resighting two species
- Occasions = 8 (throughout Dec to March sites were visited almost weekly)
- Sub-occasions= Within each occasion several re-sighting attempts (point counts) were made to try to observe the color banded individuals at points close to their capture/last resight location. Each of these point counts consisted of three intervals (5 minutes each: passive/ playback species 1/playback species 2). So, in one occasion depending on how many birds we had color banded in a site we had from 1-3 re-sighting attempts for each individual. The range 1-3 depends on re-sighting a bird, if a bird is re-sighted in attempt 1 we move on to the next bird's territory.
- Closure= This is the wintering period and you could make the assumption that it is closed. Realistically for species 1 this can be made, we had good re-sighting results but for species 2 our re-sighting and past work in the area (and literature in other sites) shows that the species moves much more, and new individuals arrive at the sites or leave the site.

- Issues: The re-sighting attempt counts are not spatially independent, they are meant to resight an individual so they are separated by ~50 meters to search within the individual's territory. Thinking ahead, we reduced the radius to 50 m to count those individuals within that radius, but we are using playback so we could be luring birds between counts. So, we made an effort to just add birds if we could see they were not the banded individuals, they had distinct plumage features(we counted one without a black cap in the previous point and this one has a black cap), and we were far from the point (>200 meters)

-Efforts in exploration= I've tried to select only the 1st count of the day at each occasion/site but this loses a lot of detections. Since I only have 8 sites, I imagine that having a collection of detections and variability is important, so I would prefer to minimize the data loss.

I've thought about collapsing data into 1s and 0s per occasion/site and then using the data in an occupancy model but if I do that I have mostly 1s in my data set. And I don't know the best way to add observation specific covariates if I collapse the data because each re-sighting attempt has its own information (amount of trees/density of vegetation, time of day).

I look forward to reading if you think these data are adequate to estimate these parameters.
